body.en: Advanced ACT algebra includes matrices, non-linear systems, and applications of polynomial and rational functions.
Solve the non-linear system: \( y=x^2 \) and \( y=x+2 \). \[ x^2=x+2 \implies x^2-x-2=0 \implies (x-2)(x+1)=0 \implies x=2 \text{ or } x=-1. \]

caption.en: Graphical solution of the non-linear system $y = x^2$ and $y = x + 2$. The line intersects the upward parabola at precisely two coordinate points: $(-1, 1)$ and $(2, 4)$.

body.en: Key log laws: \(\log_b(xy) = \log_b x + \log_b y\); \(\log_b(x/y) = \log_b x - \log_b y\); \(\log_b(x^n) = n\log_b x\). To solve \(a^{f(x)} = b\): take \(\log\) of both sides. Change of base: \(\log_b x = \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln b}\).

label.en: Worked example — Solving a logarithmic equation
▲ ACT Math 2 Traps & Pitfalls — Matrices & Advanced Systems

body.en:
• Matrix Multiplication Order & Dimensions: To compute \(AB\), the number of columns in \(A\) (inner dimension) must equal the number of rows in \(B\): \((m imes k) imes (k imes n) = (m imes n)\). Furthermore, \(AB eq BA\) in general — matrix multiplication is non-commutative!
  • Determinant & Singularity: For \(A = egin{pmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{pmatrix}\), \(\det(A) = ad - bc\). The matrix inverse \(A^{-1}\) exists if and only if \(\det(A) eq 0\). If \(\det(A) = 0\), the corresponding linear system has either no unique solution (inconsistent or dependent).
  • Extraneous Solutions in Rational Equations: When clearing denominators by multiplying by a common multiple, values that make any original denominator equal to zero are extraneous and must be discarded.
  • Logarithm Bases & Power Properties: Remember \(\log_b(A + B) eq \log_b A + \log_b B\). The addition rule applies only inside the logarithm: \(\log_b(AB) = \log_b A + \log_b B\).

question.en: Solve for \(x\): \(3^{x+1} = 5^x\). Give your answer in terms of logarithms.

Let matrices \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}\). (a) Compute the matrix product \(AB\). (b) Calculate \(\det(A)\), \(\det(B)\), and verify that \(\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B)\).

solution.en:
(a) Matrix product \(AB\): \[ AB = \begin{pmatrix} (3)(1) + (-1)(0) & (3)(5) + (-1)(-2) \\ (2)(1) + (4)(0) & (2)(5) + (4)(-2) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 15 + 2 \\ 2 & 10 - 8 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 17 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. \]

(b) Determinant calculation: \(\det(A) = (3)(4) - (-1)(2) = 12 + 2 = 14\). \(\det(B) = (1)(-2) - (5)(0) = -2\). Then \(\det(A)\det(B) = 14(-2) = -28\). From the product: \(\det(AB) = (3)(2) - (17)(2) = 6 - 34 = -28\). Thus \(\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B) = -28\). \(\checkmark\)
